For immunoblotting, the following antibodies were used: p300 (Invitrogen: MA1-16608, 1:500); AR (Abcam: ab133273, 1:1,000); H2BK20ac (Cell Signaling Technology: 34156S, 1:1,000); H2BK16ac (Abcam: ab177427, 1:1,000); H3K27ac (Cell Signaling Technology: 8173S, 1:1,000); H2B (Active Motif: 39210, 1:1,000); H3 (Cell Signaling Technology: 3638S, 1:1,000); MYC (Cell Signaling Technology: 9402S, 1:1,000); KLK3/PSA (Dako: A0562, 1:1,000); NKX3-1 (Cell Signaling Technology: 83700S, 1:1,000); CCND1 (Abcam: ab16663, 1:1,000); vinculin (Cell Signaling Technology: 18799S, 1:1,000); GAPDH (Santa Cruz Biotechnology: sc-47724, 1:1,000); BRD4 (Bethyl Laboratories: A700-004CF, 1:1,000); AR-V7 (Cell Signaling Technology: 19672S, 1:1,000); HA tag (Cell Signaling Technology: 3724S, 1:1,000); CBP (Abcam: ab253202, 1:1,000); and V5 (Invitrogen, R960-25, 1:1,000). Horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated goat anti-rabbit (Bio-Rad; 1:10,000) and goat anti-mouse (Bio-Rad; 1:5,000) secondary antibodies were used.

For ChIP–seq, the following antibodies were used: H3K27ac (Diagenode: C15410196, 1 µg per million cells); p300 (Active Motif: 61401, 2 µg per million cells); H2BK20ac (Cell Signaling Technology: 34156S, 1 µg per million cells); AR (Abcam: ab108341, 2 µg per million cells); FOXA1 (Thermo Fisher Scientific: PA5-27157, 2 µg per million cells); BRD4 (Diagenode: C15410337, 2 µg per million cells); ERG (Cell Signaling Technology: 97249S, 2 µg per million cells); RNA Pol II (Diagenode: C15200253, 1 µg per million cells); CBP (Abcam: ab253202, 2 µg per million cells); SRC2 (Cell Signaling Technology: 96687S, 4 µl per million cells) and PR (Cell Signaling Technology: 8757S, 4 µl per million cells).

For immunoprecipitation, acetylated-lysine antibody (Cell Signaling Technology: 9441S) was used at 1 µg per 100 µg of lysate.

For immunofluorescent staining (COMET-mIF) and PLA assay, the following antibodies were used: p300 (Invitrogen: 33-7600, 1:150); CBP (Invitrogen: PA5-27369, 1:150); AR (Abcam: ab133273, 1:400); H3K27ac (Cell Signaling Technology: 8173S, 1:100); Ki-67 (Abcam: ab243878, 1:300); H2BK20ac (Abcam: ab177430, 1:250); CK8 (Abcam: ab53280, 1:50); ERG (Abcam: ab92513, 1:200); PSA (Cell Marque: 324M-16, 1:50); and MYC (Abcam: ab32072, 1:50).

For ELISA, the following antibodies were used: p300 (Cell Signaling Technology: 86377S, 1:1,000); and AR (Thermo Fisher Scientific: MA5-13426, 1:50).

VCaP cells were seeded at a density of 10,000 cells per well, and all other prostate cancer cell lines were seeded at 3,000 cells per well in poly-d-lysine-coated 96-well plates (Corning) and maintained at 37 °C with 5% CO2. After 24 h, cells were treated with a serial dilution of test compounds, with 6 replicate wells for each concentration. Following 120 h of incubation, cell viability was determined using the CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Assay (Promega) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Luminescence was measured on an Infinite M1000 Pro plate reader (Tecan) and data were analysed using GraphPad Prism (v10; GraphPad Software).

A total of 4,000 VCaP cells or 1,500 LNCaP cells per well were seeded into poly-d-lysine-coated 96-well plates. After 24 h of incubation, cells were treated with a fixed concentration (100 nM) or serial dilutions of compounds and incubated for 4 h. The medium was then removed, and cells were washed three times with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) before fresh medium containing either vehicle or compounds was added. Phase-contrast images were collected every 4 h, and cell proliferation was quantified by measuring the percentage of confluence (phase object area).

Cells were lysed in RIPA buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 1× Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and denatured in NuPAGE 1× LDS sample buffer containing a reducing agent (Invitrogen) by incubation at 70 °C for 15 min. Protein concentrations were determined using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Equal amounts of protein (15–30 µg) were resolved on NuPAGE 3–8% Tris-Acetate or 4–12% Bis-Tris protein gels (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and transferred onto 0.45-µm nitrocellulose membranes (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the iBlot 3 Dry Blotting System (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Membranes were blocked in TBS-T (Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20) containing 5% non-fat dry milk for 1 h at room temperature and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies. After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and imaged using an Odyssey CLx Imager (LI-COR Biosciences). Supplementary Figure 1 shows the full, uncropped blots with molecular weight markers for all immunoblot experiments.

The binding affinities of test compounds to AR and CBP/p300 were measured using fluorescence polarization-based competitive binding assays. AR binding was assessed using the PolarScreen Androgen Receptor Competitor Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A15880) following the manufacturer’s instructions.

CBP/p300 fluorescence polarization assays were performed in 96-well plates (MTP96VPWB-EP, Eppendorf) using a CLARIOstar microplate reader (BMG Labtech). Serial dilutions of test compounds were incubated with fluorescein-labelled tracer (2 nM final) and CBP/p300 protein (20 nM final) in assay buffer (PBS pH 7.4 supplemented with 0.01% BGG, 0.01% Tween-20, and 2 mM DTT) to a final reaction volume of 100 µl per well. Plates were mixed for 15 min and incubated at room temperature for 1 h to reach equilibrium. Fluorescence polarization (mP units) was measured at 485 nm excitation and 530 nm emission.

For both AR and CBP/p300 assays, data analysis was performed in GraphPad Prism 10 using nonlinear regression. IC50 values were determined by fitting competition curves, and inhibition constant (Ki) values for competitive inhibitors were derived using nonlinear regression based on the Kd of the tracer and the concentrations of tracer and protein in the reaction. All fluorescence polarization experiments were conducted in duplicates across three independent biological replicates.

VCaP or LNCaP cells were seeded in poly-d-lysine-coated 100 mm culture dishes (Corning) and incubated overnight. Cells were incubated with the DMSO control or indicated compounds for 4 h at 37 °C before being collected and washed once with PBS. The cell suspension was then distributed into PCR tubes (50 µl per tube) and exposed to a predefined temperature gradient for 3 min using a Veriti Thermal Cycler (Applied Biosystems). Following equilibration to room temperature, cells were lysed by three freeze–thaw cycles in liquid nitrogen. Insoluble protein aggregates were pelleted by centrifugation at 20,000g for 20 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatants containing soluble proteins were recovered for western blot analysis.

All modelling and simulations were performed with Schrödinger 2025-2 (Schrödinger). Because co-crystal structures of the LBD of AR in an open antagonist conformation were not available, we used our previously reported pseudo-open model58. The bound AR ligand was modified to generate JZY3221, the AR ligand used in our design of DALTACs. To model the p300-BRD interaction with GNE-049, we used the CBP-BRD–GNE-781 co-crystal structure (Protein Data Bank (PDB) 5W0E) as the starting structure59. CBP and p300 are highly homologous proteins, especially in their BRDs, which share conserved sequence and structures. Both proteins were prepared for further modelling using the Protein Preparation Wizard60.

We used the following structures as inputs to generate the initial AR–DALTAC-1–p300 complex: (1) AR in complex with JZY3221; (2) the p300 complex with GNE-049; and (3) JZY3032 (DALTAC-1) prepared with LigPrep module61. These inputs were submitted to Generate Degrader Complex (default settings: MCMM 10,000 steps, maximum clashes 5, maximum poses 50) to construct the ternary AR–JZY3032–p300 complex. The top 20 predicted complexes were further refined using Prime62. The top-scoring ternary complex was then selected for molecular dynamics simulations.

To perform molecular dynamics simulations, the predicted ternary complex was solvated in an explicit water box with periodic boundary conditions. A cubic box was constructed with a 10 Å buffer between solute and box edge and filled with TIP4P water63. The OPLS4 force field was used for all components. Production dynamics used a RESPA integrator with a 2 fs time step. Temperature was maintained at 300 K with a Nosé–Hoover chain thermostat64 (relaxation time 1.0 ps). Pressure was controlled at 1 atm with a Martyna–Tobias–Klein barostat65 (relaxation time 2.0 ps). Long-range electrostatics used a 9 Å real-space cutoff with particle–mesh Ewald for reciprocal space66. One continuous 1-µs simulation was performed without restraints.

Root-mean-square deviation analysis of protein backbones and ligand position indicated that the system equilibrated after approximately 750 ns. Accordingly, trajectory analysis focused on the last 250 ns. Protein–protein interface features were defined as minimum heavy-atom distances between AR and p300. Contacts shorter than 0.5 nm (5 Å) were retained. Principal component analysis was applied to these interface distances, and components explaining 95% of the variance were kept. The reduced data were clustered with HDBSCAN (min_cluster_size 25, centroids enabled)67. For each cluster, the frame closest to the centroid in principal component analysis space was saved as a representative PDB. Cluster occupancies are reported as percentages of frames per cluster. Protein–protein interaction fingerprints were computed with Schrödinger’s analyze_trajectory_ppi.py. Clustering in this reduced dimensional space revealed two dominant populations, with the most prevalent state comprising nearly 80% of the ensemble. The interaction analysis was performed on snapshots representative of this dominant state.

MM-GBSA binding energies were estimated using Prime MM-GBSA (Schrödinger Release 2025-2; thermal_mmgbsa protocol) with the OPLS4 force field and the VSGB 2.0 implicit-solvent model68,69,70. Snapshots were sampled evenly from the final 250 ns of each trajectory, after which water molecules and ions were removed and each complex, receptor, and ligand were locally energy-minimized. The MM-GBSA binding energy was calculated as ΔGbind = Ecomplex − Ereceptor − Eligand, where ΔGbind is the estimated MM-GBSA binding energy and Ecomplex, Ereceptor and Eligand are the calculated MM-GBSA energies of the complex, receptor and ligand, respectively. For compound binding, DALTAC-1 was defined as the ligand and AR, p300, or AR + p300 as the receptor. For p300 association with the ternary complex, p300 (residues 1049–1160) was defined as the ligand and AR + DALTAC-1 as the receptor. To isolate the direct AR–p300 contribution in the induced geometry, DALTAC-1 was deleted from the same ternary snapshots, with p300 defined as the ligand and AR as the receptor. MM-GBSA values were used as model-dependent interaction-energy estimates to compare the relative stability of the modelled complexes and were not interpreted as experimental binding affinities.

AR protein was expressed according to the manufacturer’s protocol for the Expi293 PRO Expression System Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A40003643). In brief, Expi293 PRO cells were transfected with the HA–AR expression plasmid and cultured for 24 h before the addition of 1 μM R1881. The cultures were then incubated for an additional 24 h, and cells were collected 48 h post-transfection. Cell pellets were washed and collected by centrifugation at 5,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. The cells were resuspended in lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, 100 nM R1881 and 0.5% NP-40, supplemented with cOmplete EDTA-free Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Roche, 4693159001). Cells were lysed by sonication, and the lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 15,000 rpm for 40 min at 4 °C. The clarified lysate was incubated with anti-HA magnetic beads (Thermo Scientific, 88837) for 3 h at 4 °C. After binding, the beads were washed three times with wash buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, and 0.05% NP-40. Bound AR protein was eluted twice using elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 100 nM R1881 and 0.05% NP-40) supplemented with 2 mg ml−1 HA peptide (Thermo Scientific, 26184). The eluted protein was further purified by size-exclusion chromatography using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare) pre-equilibrated with gel filtration buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, 100 nM R1881, and 0.05% NP-40. Peak fractions containing purified AR protein were pooled to a final concentration of approximately 0.5 mg ml−1 and used for all subsequent studies.

For each reaction, 15 μl of anti-HA magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 88837) was blocked with 0.3% BSA in PBS for 1 h at 4 °C and washed three times with AR protein buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0; 150 mM NaCl; 0.05% NP-40) for 5 min per wash. Purified HA-tagged full-length AR (1 μg) was incubated with the blocked beads for at least 4 h at 4 °C. The beads were then washed three times with p300 protein buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.5, 300 mM NaCl, 0.04% Triton X-100, and 0.5 mM TCEP) for 10 min per wash and incubated overnight at 4 °C with purified Flag-tagged p300 (Active motif, 81858) (200 ng or 1 μg) in 350 μl of p300 protein buffer containing the indicated compounds or an equivalent volume of DMSO. Beads were subsequently washed at least three times with p300 protein buffer containing the corresponding compounds for 10 min per wash. Bound proteins were eluted in SDS–PAGE loading buffer and analysed by immunoblotting.

Anti-Flag IgG biosensors (Sartorius, 18-5187) were pre-equilibrated in assay buffer containing 25 mM HEPES-NaOH (pH 7.5), 300 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.04% Triton X-100, and 0.5 mM TCEP. N-terminal Flag-tagged full-length recombinant p300 protein (1 μg; Active Motif, 81858) was immobilized onto the biosensors at 25 °C until the binding signal reached a plateau. After immobilization, the biosensors were washed in assay buffer to remove unbound protein and minimize nonspecific binding.

The biosensors were then incubated with recombinant GST–His-tagged AR-LBD protein (Invitrogen, A15675) at varying concentrations in assay buffer containing either 10 μM DALTAC-1 or an equivalent volume of DMSO. The association phase was monitored, followed by transfer of the biosensors into assay buffer to measure dissociation. Binding data were analysed using Octet Analysis Studio 13.0 (Sartorius). Sensorgrams obtained in the presence of DMSO were used as reference controls and subtracted from those obtained with DALTAC-1. The reference-subtracted data were globally fitted to a 1:1 binding model to determine the equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd).

PLA was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Navinci Diagnostics) using the Naveni TriFlex Cell kit for cultured cells (AR–p300) and the NaveniFlex Tissue Red kit for VCaP-CRPC tumour sections.

Cultured cells (Naveni TriFlex Cell) were fixed, permeabilized and blocked per kit protocol instructions. Primary antibodies against AR (1:400) and p300 (1:200) were applied in antibody diluent and incubated as recommended. After washes, Naveni proximity probes were added, followed by ligation and rolling-circle amplification steps according to the vendor’s workflow. Slides were counterstained with DAPI and mounted in antifade medium. PLA signals were visualized on a Zeiss LSM900 fluorescence microscope under identical exposure settings across conditions.

For formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumour sections (NaveniFlex Tissue Red), sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated and subjected to heat-induced epitope retrieval as specified by the kit. After blocking, primary antibodies against AR (1:1,000) and p300 (1:100) were applied in antibody diluent and incubated per protocol. Following washes, NaveniFlex proximity probes, ligation and amplification were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI, slides were mounted and images were acquired on a Zeiss LSM900 microscope using matched acquisition parameters.

Where indicated, PLA puncta were quantified as foci per nucleus using standardized thresholds across groups.

VCaP cells were plated in 96-well plates (50,000 cells per well) and cultured for 3 days in medium containing 5% charcoal-stripped FBS. Cells were treated with a serial dilution of DALTAC-1, Neg-1, or Neg-2 compounds for 3 h. Following treatment, cells were lysed in 1× AlphaLISA SureFire Ultra Lysis Buffer (PerkinElmer) for 30 min at 4 °C with gentle mixing.

For detection, high-binding MaxiSorp 96-well plates (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were coated overnight at 4 °C with 50 µl of anti-AR antibody (clone AR441, Thermo Fisher Scientific) diluted 1:50 in PBS. After washing with TBS-T and blocking with 5% BSA for 2 h at room temperature, 50 µl of cell lysate was added to each well and incubated for 1 h at room temperature. Plates were washed three times with TBS-T and then incubated overnight at 4 °C with rabbit anti-p300 (D8Z4E, 86377, Cell Signaling Technology) antibody diluted 1:1,000 in blocking buffer.

After washing, HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (Bio-Rad, 1706515; 1:10,000 dilution) was added and incubated for 1 h at room temperature. Plates were washed seven or eight times with TBST, and chemifluorescent signals were developed using QuantaRed Enhanced Chemifluorescent HRP Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Fluorescence (excitation 570 nm, emission 585 nm) was immediately measured using a Tecan Infinite M1000 Pro plate reader, with readings taken at 5 and 15 min.

Cells (50 million) were washed once with ice-cold PBS, scraped, and pelleted at 500g for 5 min at 4 °C. The cell pellet was resuspended in 2 ml hypotonic buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl2, 0.1% Triton X-100, 15 mM β-mercaptoethanol) supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors and rotated for 1 h at 4 °C. Nuclei were collected by centrifugation at 2,000g for 5 min at 4 °C, the supernatant (cytoplasmic fraction) was discarded, and nuclei were washed once with hypotonic buffer.

The nuclear pellet was lysed in 1 ml nuclear lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 10 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl2, 0.5% Triton X-100, 15 mM β-mercaptoethanol) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors and rotated for 1 h at 4 °C. Benzonase (500 U ml−¹; Sigma-Aldrich E1014) was added during lysis to digest nucleic acids. Lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 16,000g for 20 min at 4 °C, and the supernatant was collected and precleared with 50 µl Dynabeads Protein G magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher 10004D). Protein concentration was determined using the Pierce 660 nm Protein Assay (Thermo Fisher 22660).

For each immunoprecipitation, 400 µg of precleared nuclear lysate was incubated overnight at 4 °C with either anti-androgen receptor antibody (Abcam ab108341) or anti-p300 antibody (Active Motif 61401). Antigen–antibody complexes were captured with 30 µl Dynabeads Protein G for 2 h at 4 °C. Beads were washed three times with wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 10 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl2).

For immunoblotting, bound proteins were eluted in 1× NuPAGE LDS Sample Buffer (Thermo Fisher NP0007) supplemented with 50 mM DTT and subjected to SDS–PAGE. For mass spectrometry, washed beads were flash-frozen and stored at −80 °C for subsequent on-bead trypsin digestion.

Total RNA was isolated using QIAzol Lysis Reagent (QIAGEN). In brief, 1 × 106 cells were lysed in 700 µl QIAzol and incubated for 5 min at room temperature to allow for complete dissociation of nucleoprotein complexes. Following the addition of 140 µl chloroform, samples were vigorously mixed and centrifuged at 12,000g for 15 min at 4 °C. The aqueous phase was collected, mixed with 1.5 volumes of ethanol, and applied to a RNeasy Mini spin column (QIAGEN) for purification according to the miRNeasy Mini Kit protocol. RNA was eluted in RNase-free water, and the concentration and purity were assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

For quantitative PCR analysis, cDNA was synthesized from purified RNA using the Maxima First Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. qPCR reactions were performed with SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Applied Biosystems) on a QuantStudio 7 Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems).

Primers used in this study are listed below: GAPDH forward (F): ACAACTTTGGTATCGTGGAAGG and reverse (R): GCCATCACGCCACAGTTTC; KLK3/PSA F: GACCAAGTTCATGCTGTGTGC and R: CCACTCACCTTTCCCCTCAAG; TMPRSS2 F: GTCCCCACTGTCTACGAGGT and R: CAGACGACGGGGTTGGAAG; NKX3-1 F: CCCACACTCAGGTGATCGAG and R: GAGCTGCTTTCGCTTAGTCTT; MYC F: CCTGGTGCTCCATGAGGAGAC and R: CAGACTCTGACCTTTTGCCAGG; CCND1 F: GCTGCGAAGTGGAAACCATC and R: CCTCCTTCTGCACACATTTGAA.

Tandem mass tag (TMT) proteomic analysis was performed as previously described8, with minor modifications. VCaP cells were treated with DMSO or DALTAC-1 (JZY3032) in three independent biological replicates. Cell lysates were prepared, and protein concentrations were determined. For each sample, 75 µg of protein was reduced with 5 mM dithiothreitol, alkylated with 15 mM 2-chloroacetamide, precipitated with ice-cold acetone, and digested overnight with a trypsin/Lys-C mixture at a 1:50 protease-to-protein ratio. Peptides were labelled with TMTpro 16-plex reagents (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A44521), with DMSO replicates assigned to channels 126, 127N and 128N and JZY3032 replicates assigned to channels 130C, 131C and 132C. Labelled peptides were pooled and separated into 12 fractions by high-pH reversed-phase chromatography.

Fractions were analysed at the University of Michigan Proteomics Resource Facility using an Orbitrap Ascend Tribrid mass spectrometer equipped with a FAIMS source and coupled to a Vanquish Neo UHPLC system. Peptides were separated on an Easy-Spray PepMap Neo C18 column, and data were acquired using two FAIMS compensation voltages (−45 and −65 V) and a MultiNotch MS3 method to minimize reporter-ion ratio distortion. Data were processed using Proteome Discoverer v3.0 and searched against the Swiss-Prot Homo sapiens protein database (TaxID 9606; version 5 February 2025). Peptide-spectrum matches and proteins were filtered to a false-discovery rate of ≤1%. TMT quantification was based on high-quality MS3 spectra with an average signal-to-noise ratio of ≥10 and isolation interference of <50%.

VCaP cells were treated with DMSO, 100 nM DALTAC-1 for 4 or 12 h, or a combination of p300/CBPi and ARi for 12 h, each in three biological replicates. The cells were then subjected to acetyl-lysine proteomics analysis as previously described8. In brief, total proteins were extracted, digested with trypsin, and acetylated peptides were enriched using anti–acetyl-lysine antibody–conjugated beads. Enriched peptides were analysed by nano-liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (nanoLC–MS/MS) on a Q Exactive HF mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and raw data were processed using MaxQuant (v2.3.0.0) with acetyl-lysine and protein N-terminal acetylation set as variable modifications.

In-solution digestion: VCaP cells were treated with 100 nM DALTAC-1 (JZY3032) or DMSO for 4 h. Co-immunoprecipitation assays were performed as described above. The beads were resuspended in 50 µl of 0.1 M ammonium bicarbonate buffer (pH ~8). Cysteines were reduced by adding 50 µl of 10 mM DTT and incubating at 45 °C for 30 min. Samples were cooled to room temperature and alkylation of cysteines was achieved by incubating with 65 mM 2-chloroacetamide, under darkness, for 30 min at room temperature. An overnight (~16 h) digestion with 1 µg sequencing grade, modified trypsin was carried out at 37 °C with constant shaking in a Thermomixer. Digestion was stopped by acidification and peptides were desalted using SepPak C18 cartridges using the manufacturer’s protocol (Waters). Samples were completely dried using a vacufuge. The resulting peptides were dissolved in 8 µl of 0.1% formic acid/2% acetonitrile solution, and 2 µl of the peptide solution was resolved on a nano-capillary reverse phase column (Acclaim PepMap C18, 2 µm, 50 cm, Thermo Scientific) using a 0.1% formic acid/2% acetonitrile (buffer A) and 0.1% formic acid/95% acetonitrile (buffer B) gradient at 300 nl min−1 over a period of 180 min (2–22% buffer B in 110 min, 22–40% in 25 min, 40–90% in 5 min followed by holding at 90% buffer B for 5 min and requilibration with buffer A for 25 min). The eluent was directly introduced into the Orbitrap Fusion tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) using an Easy-Spray source. MS1 scans were acquired at 120K resolution (AGC target = 106; max IT = 50 ms). Data-dependent collision induced dissociation MS/MS spectra were acquired using the Top speed method (3 s) following each MS1 scan (NCE ≈ 32%; AGC target = 105; max IT 45 ms).

Proteins were identified by searching the MS/MS data against the UniProt human database (sp_canonical TaxID=9606, v2025-02-05) using Proteome Discoverer (v3, Thermo Scientific). Search parameters included MS1 mass tolerance of 10 ppm and fragment tolerance of 0.2 Da; two missed cleavages were allowed. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was considered a fixed modification and oxidation of methionine, deamidation of asparagine and glutamine were considered as potential modifications. The false-discovery rate (FDR) was determined using Percolator, and proteins or peptides with a FDR of ≤1% were retained for further analysis.

VCaP cells were treated with 100 nM DALTAC-1 or a combination of 100 nM p300/CBPi and ARi for 4, 12 or 24 h, each in two biological replicates. The cells were then subjected to RNA-seq as previously described8. In brief, total RNA was extracted, and ribosomal RNA was removed using the RiboErase module of the KAPA RNA HyperPrep Kit (Roche). rRNA-depleted RNA was used for library preparation following the manufacturer’s protocol, and libraries were quality-checked on an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer before sequencing on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform (paired-end, 2× 100 bp). Sequencing reads were quantified with Kallisto (v0.50.1), normalized with edgeR (v3.34.1), and analysed for differential expression using limma-voom (v3.58.1). GSEA was performed using fgsea (v1.28.0), and data visualization employed tidyverse, gplots, ggplot2, gtable (v0.3.0), and EnhancedVolcano (v1.15.0) packages in R.

ChIP–seq was performed as previously described8. In brief, cells were cross-linked in 1% formaldehyde, quenched with glycine, and lysed for chromatin extraction. Chromatin was sheared to 200–600 bp fragments using a Bioruptor (Diagenode) and subjected to immunoprecipitation with antibodies against transcription factors (AR, FOXA1, p300, ERG and BRD4) or histone marks (H3K27ac, H2BK20ac and RNA Pol II) using the iDeal ChIP–seq Kit (Diagenode). Drosophila spike-in chromatin (Active Motif, 53083) and spike-in antibody (Active Motif, 61686) were added during the overnight incubation. After reverse cross-linking and DNA purification, sequencing libraries were prepared and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform. For PR, SRC2, and CBP ChIP–seq, we performed double-cross-linking. In brief, 10 million cells were cross-linked with 250 μl of 200 mM DSP (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 22585) for 30 min at room temperature. PBS was then added to a final volume of 9 ml, followed by 40 μl of 0.5 M EDTA. Formaldehyde (250 μl, 37%) was added, and the cells were incubated for an additional 10 min at room temperature. Cross-linking was quenched by adding 1 ml of 1.25 M glycine and 200 μl of 10% Tween-20, followed by incubation for 5 min. Samples were then processed according to the ChIP–seq protocol described previously.

ChIP–seq reads were trimmed using Trimmomatic (v0.39). Alignment was then performed separately to both the human genome (hg38) and the Drosophila genome (dm6) using BWA (v0.7.17-r1198-dirty). Low-quality and duplicate reads were filtered with SAMtools and Picard, respectively. Normalization ratios were calculated based on the lowest amount of uniquely aligned reads per ChIP target to each genome as recommended on the vendor’s website. Reads were then downsampled per the normalization ratios. Peak calling was then performed with MACS2 (v2.1.1.20160309) using narrow or broad settings depending on the target, and blacklisted genomic regions were removed using BEDTools with the ENCODE exclusion list. Motif enrichment analysis was performed using HOMER (v4.10). Processed data were converted to BigWig format using UCSC wigToBigWig for visualization.

Read density heat maps and average enrichment profiles were generated using deepTools. For histone marks, signals were plotted within ±2.5 kb of the reference point, and for transcription factors within ±1 kb. The parameters --skipZeros, --averageType mean, and --plotType se were applied. ENCODE blacklist regions (ENCFF356LFX) were excluded from analysis. Genomic interval operations were performed using the IRanges Bioconductor package (v2.36.0), and non-promoter regions were defined using the ChIPseeker R package tool annotatePeak excluding ±1 kb windows surrounding annotated gene transcription start site regions. Peak overlap and annotation analyses were additionally performed using the ChIPpeakAnno R package (v3.6.5).

Mouse prostate organoids and patient-derived xenograft organoids were established and maintained following previously described protocols41,71. In brief, organoids were cultured in 50 µl Matrigel domes and overlaid with prostate organoid medium, with media changed every 2–3 days and passaging performed weekly. For growth and drug-response assays, organoid fragments were dissociated into single cells and used to generate new organoids (1,000 cells per dome for standard viability assays) in complete organoid medium. Cell viability was measured using the CellTiter-Glo 3D assay (Promega) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

All animal procedures were approved by the University of Michigan Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC; protocol PRO0001291) and performed in accordance with institutional guidelines. Male CB17 SCID mice, 4–6 weeks old, were procured from the breeding colony at the University of Michigan and maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions on a 12 h light:12 h dark cycle, with ambient temperature maintained at 18–23 °C and relative humidity maintained at 40–60%. Only male mice were used, as prostate cancer is specific to males.

Sample sizes for efficacy studies (n = 7–20 tumours per group) were chosen prospectively based on a power calculation: with >7 tumours per group, the study had an estimated 92.3% power to detect a 50% decrease in mean tumour volume or metastatic burden, assuming a coefficient of variation of 40%. No animals or data points were excluded from analysis. Mice were randomly assigned to treatment groups prior to dosing. Histopathological evaluation and immunohistochemistry-based scoring for drug toxicity studies were performed in a blinded manner by two independent pathologists; blinding was applied to other end-points (for example, tumour volume measurement). Per IACUC protocol PRO0001291, tumour burden was not permitted to exceed 4,186 mm3, and this limit was not exceeded in any experiment reported here.

Male SCID mice (6–8 weeks old) were obtained from the breeding colony at the University of Michigan and maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions. All animal procedures were approved by the University of Michigan IACUC (protocol PRO0001291). Subcutaneous xenograft tumours were established by injecting 3 × 106 VCaP cells suspended in serum-free medium mixed 1:1 with Matrigel (BD Biosciences) into both dorsal flanks. Tumour growth was monitored weekly using digital calipers, and volumes were calculated as (π/6) × (length × width2). At study end-points, mice were euthanized, and tumours were excised and weighed.

The castration-resistant VCaP model was generated as previously described8. In brief, mice were castrated once tumours reached 150–200 mm³, and treatment with DALTAC-1 (30 mg kg−1 intraperitoneally or 60 mg kg−1 orally), combination of p300/CBPi (30 mg kg−1 orally) and ARi (10 mg kg−1 orally), or vehicle was initiated after tumour regrowth to baseline size for 24 days.

A tissue microarray (TMA) was created according to a design involving 8 unique cases from 4 different subgroups: vehicle (n = 2), p300/CBPi + ARi (n = 2), DALTAC-1 intraperitoneal (n = 2) and DALTAC-1 oral administration (n = 2). Two independent samples were selected from each subgroup. To ensure data reliability and representativeness, a replicate core from each sample was included in the TMA, resulting in a focused 16-core TMA. Technical details are as follows: in brief, FFPE donor blocks for the selected samples were chosen by two study pathologists (R.M. and S.M.) after reviewing the haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. The pathologists then annotated the H&E slides to identify the most representative tumour area of interest (AOI) on the surface of each donor block. The Semiautomatic tissue arrayer from Beecher Instruments (Sun Prairie) was used to punch 1 mm-diameter cores from each marked region. These cores were carefully transferred into a recipient acrylic block in a grid-like pattern. Once transferred, the recipient block was incubated at 37 °C for 30 min to ensure proper fusion of the cores within the paraffin. The prepared TMA block was then sectioned at 4-μm thickness and stained with H&E to assess the quality of the final TMA.

Four-micrometre-thick sections from the PDX TMA, mounted on positively charged slides, were cut and prepared according to the guidelines and recommendations. Subsequently, the slides were deparaffinized using a standard xylene and graded ethanol series, followed by heat-induced epitope retrieval (HIER) as per the Lunaphore COMET protocol to unmask target epitopes72. Automated sequential immunofluorescence (seqIF) staining was performed on the COMET instrument (Lunaphore) to enable highly multiplexed protein detection with the target primary antibodies. This process involved cycles of staining, imaging, and elution managed by the COMET Control software through controlled temperature and microfluidic reagent delivery. Each cycle included incubation with unconjugated primary antibodies, followed by species-specific fluorescently conjugated secondary antibodies (for example, Alexa Fluor 555 and 647), automated image acquisition including DAPI counterstaining, and complete antibody removal via elution. After the final staining cycle, the COMET Control software (v1.5.0.0) automatically stitched, aligned, and stacked images to produce a single OME-TIFF file for each sample. During post-processing, autofluorescence background was systematically subtracted using reference images acquired from unstained tissue sections at the beginning of the protocol.

The raw prostate TMA data included single-cell measurements across multiple markers along with their spatial locations. Markers were grouped into two panels based on biological relevance, as shown in the plots. To normalize marker expression and reduce skewness, a log1p transformation (log1p(expression)) was applied. Outliers were identified and removed separately for each marker within each group. Outliers were defined as values exceeding ±5 median absolute deviations from the group-specific median. The median absolute deviation is a robust measure of statistical dispersion that calculates the median of the absolute deviations from the median, making it less sensitive to extreme outliers than standard deviation. This approach preserves most of the data while minimizing the impact of extreme values.

The prostate cancer PDX models MDA-PCa-146-12 and MDA-PCa-183 were established and maintained as previously described8. MDA-PCa-146-12 is an AR+ and ERG+ adenocarcinoma PDX derived from the adenocarcinoma region of a primary prostate tumour with mixed adenocarcinoma–neuroendocrine morphology. MDA-PCa-183 is an AR+ and ERG+ adenocarcinoma PDX derived from a bone marrow aspirate of a treatment-naive patient with metastatic prostate cancer. Both models harbour PTEN loss and TP53 loss-of-function alterations. In brief, tumour fragments (~2 mm3) were implanted subcutaneously into the dorsal flanks of six- to eight-week-old male SCID mice bred in-house and propagated by serial passage. Once tumours reached approximately 200 mm3 using the formula (π/6) × (length × width²), mice were randomized into treatment groups. Mice bearing MDA-PCa-146-12 tumours received vehicle or DALTAC-1 (30 mg kg−1, intraperitoneally three times per week). Mice bearing MDA-PCa-183 tumours received vehicle, DALTAC-1 (30 mg kg−1, intraperitoneally three times per week), ARV-766 (10 mg kg−1, orally, 5 times per week), or enzalutamide (10 mg kg−1, orally, 5 times per week). Tumour volumes were measured weekly, and all procedures were conducted in accordance with protocols approved by the University of Michigan Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC, protocol PRO0001291).

All experimental procedures and statistical analyses were performed as previously described8. In brief, key experiments were independently repeated at least three times, with most quantitative assays carried out in biological replicates as noted. Representative images and immunoblots reflect reproducible results, and the number of biological replicates is provided in the figure legends. No data were excluded from analysis. For in vitro experiments, sample sizes were not predetermined by a statistical method and randomization was not applicable, as cells were allocated to experimental conditions under homogeneous culture conditions. For animal studies, sample sizes were determined prospectively (see Methods), and mice were randomly assigned to treatment groups. Histopathological and immunohistochemical scoring for drug toxicity studies were performed in a blinded manner by two independent pathologists; all other data collection and quantification relied on automated instruments or standardized computational pipelines and were therefore not blinded. Two-sided statistical tests were used unless otherwise stated. Comparisons between two groups used unpaired t-tests or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, and multiple comparisons were corrected using the Benjamini–Hochberg method. Exact P values are reported in the figure legends.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

All data are available in the manuscript and Supplementary information. Raw sequencing data (RNA-seq and ChIP–seq) have been deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession numbers GSE310948 and GSE310949. This study used the following public databases and reference datasets: human reference genome (GRCh38/hg38), used for ChIP–seq read alignment (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/assembly/GCF_000001405.26/). Drosophila melanogaster reference genome (dm6), used for ChIP–seq spike-in normalization (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/assembly/GCF_000001215.4/). The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifiers PXD084247, PXD084250 and PXD084305. Protein Data Bank (PDB) entry 5W0E (CBP-BRD–GNE-781 co-crystal structure) was used as the structural template for computational modelling of the p300-BRD–GNE-049 interaction. No restrictions apply to the availability of these data. Source data are provided with this paper.

No custom code or software was used in this study. All computational analyses were performed using publicly available software and code, which are described in Methods.

J.L., J.Y., S.W. and A.M.C. conceived and designed the studies. J.L. performed all of the in vitro and functional genomics experiments with assistance from S.D., J.C., Y.L., X.J., X.W., K.G., S.E. and M.W. Y.Q., J.C.Y.-T. and J.L. performed all of the organoid and animal efficacy studies with assistance from S.E., Y.Y. and A.J.T. E.Y. and S.L. carried out all of the bioinformatics analyses with assistance from A.P. J.T. and J.Y. performed the computational modelling of the AR–p300–DALTAC-1 complex. R.M. and S.M. carried out all of the histopathological evaluations of drug toxicity as well as quantified all of the histology-based data. R.M. and S.M. carried out all of the immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence staining. R.S. and A.R. conducted quantification of sequential multiplex immunofluorescence datasets. X.C. and F.S. performed sequencing. J.Y., W.X., M.W., S.J. and S.W. designed, synthesized and performed initial evaluations of a large number of DALTAC molecules, leading to the discovery of DALTAC-1, as well as Neg-1 and Neg-2 control compounds. J.L., J.Y., S.J.M., J.C.Y.-T., S.W. and A.M.C. wrote the manuscript and organized the final figures.

Violin plots showing the log10-transformed expression levels of individual targets across single cells based on Seq-mIF staining from PD5 tumors in the VCaP-CRPC study (n = 462,056 cells for veh, n = 501,827 cells for p300/CBPi+ARi, n = 597,031 cells for DALTAC-1 i.p and n = 464,670 cells for DALTAC-1 p.o). #1367. Alisson, 34, reveals he wants to STAY at Liverpool after rolling back the years against Crystal Palace... but is extending the goalkeeper's contract the right call, asks LEWIS STEELE

Published: 07:00 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 13:09 EST, 10 November 2026

Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson Becker insists he wants to stay at the club after his contract expires at the end of this season.

The Brazilian, now 34, put in a throwback performance in the Reds’ win at Crystal Palace on Sunday with some fine stops to keep his side in the game at 0-0 before the big-money attackers did their job at the other end.

It came after a period where Alisson has been questioned by fans for a string of errors in what is his final contracted year at the club. And the No1 has now opened up on his future for the first time.

Asked if he wants to stay beyond the end of the season, Alisson said: ‘Yes, in my mind. I’m focused on playing every game but in my mind I’m happy to stay. You know, that depends on a lot of aspects and different situations.

‘But my will is to stay. I’m happy here, my family is happy here. I’m still hungry for titles and for delivering good performances. I still want to play at the top level for as long as I can. So that’s my thinking on that.’

Alisson later added that his agent has held talks with the club over a new deal.

The 34-year-old keeper will spend the next week resting after not being called up by Brazil for the second straight international window

The keeper will spend the next week resting after not being called up by Brazil for the second straight international window, which he admits is a decision taken somewhat beyond his will.

He said: ‘It is beneficial (not going), for sure. You have to use it right because you have a lot of time so if you don’t train, if you don’t prepare, time goes really quick and you need to stay sharp.

‘It’s not that I will sit on the couch for a week and then come back training. I still have to work hard but in my mind I can use the time to relax and be more with my family.

‘It’s a little bit against my will. What I always want is to be with the national team but I understand this is what I have at the moment and I will use this time and take the benefit from the rest.’

Should Liverpool continue in Alisson wonderland?

It is tempting to just say ‘yes’ and end this debate there.

Alisson is still the best goalkeeper Liverpool have on their books and, even though he is maybe not as solid as he once was, the 34-year-old remains one of the best goalkeepers in the world.

Last summer, he flirted with the idea of leaving and seriously considered a move to Juventus. Alisson speaks fluent Italian from his time at AS Roma and held talks with the Turin club over a return.

But Liverpool triggered a clause in his deal to extend his stay by a year. With several big names leaving such as Mohamed Salah, Andy Robertson, Ibrahima Konate and Curtis Jones, the club did not want another experienced head to depart and leave a leadership vacuum.

They have also spent the last three years succession planning for Alisson’s long-term replacement and have signed a number of goalkeepers for more than £60million combined.

Giorgi Mamardashvili is the most obvious in the pecking order. He has had mixed reviews with fans but the Georgian is appreciated more internally than maybe externally. The club believes he has several levels left to step up.

Lucca Brughmans will join from Belgian side Genk after a £28.3million deal was struck. Liverpool genuinely think he is the best goalkeeper on the market and they fought off stiff competition from Real Madrid to sign him.

Liverpool think Lucca Brughmans - who will join them from Belgian side Genk - is the best goalkeeper on the market and they fought off stiff competition from Real Madrid to sign him

They have also signed highly-rated Armin Pecsi and England youth goalkeeper Zach Trinder from Wolves.

Clearly, the post-Alisson future is sorted, with some of them tipped to go far in the game. But are any of them better than Alisson now? No. Will any of them be better next season? No.

Alisson missed 54 games across the previous two seasons with injury and illness, according to Transfermarkt, but his omission from Brazil camps and a specialised pre-season programme mean the keeper seems to have put his issues behind him. Touch wood.

For that reason, a one-year extension makes sense – for both Alisson and 35-year-old captain Virgil van Dijk. The club will have to face up to a future without both of their defensive stalwarts but, for now, they remain the best in class.

#1366. Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs

Manchester United fans were never going to pass up the opportunity to aim a volley of abuse in the direction of their bitter rivals.

By the end of another deeply unconvincing performance, though, they were more preoccupied by the problems afflicting their own team than the cheating scandal engulfing Manchester City.

Against City at Old Trafford last month, United lost to a team who were down to 10 men after just 23 minutes.

This time around they could not hold on to a lead against a Tottenham Hotspur side also navigating a numerical disadvantage following Rodrigo Bentancur’s sending off.

Rodrigo Bentancur dives in on Luke Shaw and it's all kicking off at Old Trafford! 🫨 https://t.co/uJUAMuZNzc

The sum total of it all is that United have now made their worst start to a season for 40 years, which is saying something given the traumas of the post-Ferguson era, and perhaps more disconcertingly, look to all intents and purposes like a team going backwards.

The bounce they enjoyed under Michael Carrick last season en route to Champions League qualification is over and, after just six points from as many games, it is hard to shake the feeling that it is going to be anything but a serious battle to finish in the top four or five.

The supporters did not hide their disgruntlement. There were boos around the half hour mark after an insipid opening when Spurs did everything but score and a slow, sluggish, dishevelled United almost looked impervious to their troubles.

Carrick had called for his players to show some “fire” coming into this match, but instead watched them ambling around like it was all a terrible inconvenience. The ease with which Spurs ran around them was alarming. There were more jeers at the interval and again at full time.

Carrick admitted that “hurt” although not as much you suspect as the sight of players feigning interest and then throwing away three points when they had finally summoned some fight to lead courtesy of Bryan Mbeumo’s goal.

Bryan Mbeumo slots it home to give Manchester United the lead against Spurs! 🎯 https://t.co/7yKnpyhfUe

It was a lovely finish after good work by the largely anonymous Matheus Cunha, and when Bentancur was sent off five minutes later after butting Luke Shaw, it should have been the cue to see out the game. To fail to do so against a side as toothless as Tottenham made it all the worse. Leading late on against Everton last month, they also failed to get over the line. It cannot keep happening.

Equally, United cannot play like they did in the first half here when they face Atlético Madrid in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night or at Elland Road against bitter rivals Leeds five days later and expect to get anything from either game. They are not the sort of matches Carrick would want with his team in this shape, but they need to find some inspiration from somewhere.

Carlos Baleba coming on around the hour mark and making a difference on his debut will at least offer Carrick some grounds for encouragement. The £65m midfield signing from Brighton offers some energy and urgency and looks a more natural bedfellow for Kobbie Mainoo than Youri Tielemans, who was woeful against Spurs and should have come off earlier.

In truth, Tielemans was not alone. Throughout the team there was a disconnect and unease and Carrick admitted it became contagious.

“We just couldn’t find a way to get ourselves into the game, whether that was with the ball or without the ball,” the United manager said. “We were a little bit slow with the decision-making, didn’t quite see the passing areas, the space. You don’t want it to happen, but sometimes it can and it probably spread through the team a little bit too much.”

It does not help that Bruno Fernandes is being hampered by an injury he has been carrying for weeks or that Carrick has no natural centre-forward to call upon with Benjamin Sesko again sidelined by the recurrence of a worrying shin problem. Amad Diallo did return here after a lengthy lay-off of his own, but did not look match fit.

In defence, Lisandro Martínez did enough to put off Dominic Solanke, who fired over from Sávio’s cross in the second half, but this was otherwise another poor showing from the Argentine centre-back, one of several positions where United need upgrades.

United needed shaking badly, but when Carrick turned to his bench he called upon Joshua Zirkzee, a fitful forward the club wanted to sell this summer, and right-back Diogo Dalot in addition to Baleba.

Marcus Rashford cannot have been fit given he was only introduced in the 95th minute and perhaps the same was true of the unused Mason Mount. As for £50m summer signing Andrey Santos, this was another league game when the Brazilian midfielder did not get a look in.

United fans had taunted Spurs when a goal and a man up. “You’re going down with the City,” they crowed, a nod to the possibility of City being expelled or relegated from the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching more than 100 financial rules.

United fans had also revived their Stretford End “ticker” after reaching the conclusion that none of City’s titles under Abu Dhabi ownership had been won fairly so, in their eyes, it is now 50 years since their rivals last won anything legitimately. City, of course, continue to maintain their innocence and have lodged an appeal.

But United fans were unable to crow for too long once Solanke levelled.

Spurs are level in stoppage-time! 😳 https://t.co/NoivNchgWw

It had been similar early in the game when the home fans had trained their sights on City. “You cheating b--------, you know what you are”, they sang lustily.

But as the match wore on, those chants began to quieten as the crowd, taking their lead from the team, fell decidedly flat.

Carrick is going to have to find a spark from somewhere and quickly.

Speaking to BBC Match of the Day, Carrick said: “It was a mixed game. We found it tough to start with. For a number of reasons, we were not quite there. You could see it was a challenging time.

“But the lads grew into the game, in the second half I thought we were better in everything. To get the game as we wanted it, in such a good position - we should see it through. We have to manage those situations. That’s two late goals which have hurt us, and things look very different. That’s the reality.”

When asked about the boos at half-time and full-time, he replied: “It’s not nice, it hurts a lot because I care about this club. But I understand the disappointment, the reality is what it is, we need to get back to winning games.”

3 - Manchester United have failed to win any of their last three Premier League games against sides that have received a red card (D1 L2). Disadvantage? https://t.co/DuSpvymZfu

The Tottenham boss told Sky Sports: “I think we played very well against a great team. We had many chances to score in the first half. Three or four. The second half is normal to suffer against this quality. I am very happy because I have seen the right spirit and character.

We have to react in all ways we can. It is a bad way, it is not the right way. I kiss Bentancur in the dressing room. Football is character.

“We win the game if we play as a team. We didn’t win this game playing as a team. Every game like today, we will win many games.”

When asked about Solanke, he replied: “He is a good player for Tottenham. There for not too many strikers better than Solanke. Today he was captain because he deserved it, especially in this moment because he suffer because Tottenham didn’t score or win any games. He is a great guy, great player and we are behind him.

“We have to believe in ourselves and this football way. If we believe, improve and play as a team, we will score many goals and win many games. If we don’t play as a team, it is impossible.”

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League game between Manchester United and Tottenham at Old Trafford.

If Manchester City had not entered a legal battle with the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching 114 charges relating to financial regulations by an independent panel, then surely there would be more pressure on the two head coaches in the dugout this evening?

Man Utd and Tottenham have undoubtedly both endured extremely disappointing starts to their respective top-flight campaigns. The hosts sit just inside the bottom half of the table after picking up just five points from their opening five matches. It’s going even worse for Tottenham, who languish in 20th with zero wins and just two points.

The perilous landscape leaves only one reasonable conclusion: this has all the ingredients for an early season six-pointer.

The strain is perhaps less intense on Michael Carrick, with the Englishman having built up a bundle of goodwill after cleaning up the mess left by Ruben Amorim last season as Man Utd eventually finished third, qualifying for the Champions League. Fans were left slightly underwhelmed by the club’s transfer window, with the players at Carrick’s disposal having not forged any momentum so far in this campaign.

The spotlight is definitely shining more intensely upon Roberto De Zerbi after big-spending Tottenham splashed over £300m in the summer on the likes of Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Jan Paul van Hecke and Savio. However, the Italian boss is yet to strike the correct rhythm with his newly-formed squad. An encouraging performance backed up by a positive result here at Old Trafford could be the perfect antidote to ease the worries of fans fearing that Tottenham could be embroiled in another relegation battle.

All eyes are on this one. Kick-off is at 17:30, with team news coming shortly.

#1364. Jude Bellingham says he 'wants to be a gentleman' but admits he doesn't feel 'mature' because 'I can't cook, I can't drive and I rely on my family' in new smouldering photoshoot

Published: 10:54 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 13:36 EST, 10 November 2026

Real Madrid and England star Jude Bellingham has admitted he doesn't feel 'mature', despite being labelled as such from a young age.

The midfielder, 23, has impressed with his level head and assured public speaking since breaking onto the professional scene at 16 and living under the glare of the public eye in his formative years.

But Bellingham has confessed that his complete attention to detail as a footballer has left deficiencies in other areas of his life, such as cooking or driving.

Speaking to Vogue in an interview accompanying a fashion photoshoot in which he's dressed to fit the 60s and 70s aesthetic he leans into, Bellingham also spoke about his desire to be a role model for the younger generation.

'I feel mature in a football context because I’ve played nearly 400 games, but in a life context I don’t feel that mature now, to be honest,' he told Vogue.

'I can’t cook, I can’t drive… I’m good at what I do, but everything else? Not that great. I rely on my friends, my family to help me do stuff – chef, cleaner, mum, whoever else.

Jude Bellingham poses for Vogue during a photoshoot displaying his love of 60s fashion

Bellingham admits he isn't mature in some areas of his life - seen here holding up his provisional driving licence

'That’s where I’m at. I work hard every day and all day, and then when I get home, I’ve probably neglected learning how to do some of the more basic things. But there’ll be a time and a place for that, I’m sure.'

Bellingham plays with a fierce competitive spirit on the pitch but is aware of his responsibility to behave away from football, adding: 'I’ve always said that, off the pitch, I want to be a gentleman.'

The Real superstar, who is in a relationship with American influencer and model Ashlyn Castro, went on: 'You can’t just behave how you want but then still represent a city or a country every time you wear their shirt, because you are inspiring [someone].

'Whether you like it or not, you are looked up to by the next generation. I prefer to see it as a privilege.'

The photoshoot for the fashion magazine showcased Bellingham's sense of style, which he says is rooted in his admiration for iconic characters from the 60s and 70s such as Elvis Presley, Michael Caine and James Bond movies of the era.

The Vogue cover shows Bellingham in a dark brown suit and coat with wide lapels and a bright orange cardigan, while he appears in a herringbone overcoat and white chino shorts in another.

Another image shows Bellingham holding up his green provisional driving licence.

Bellingham, selected in the England squad for upcoming internationals against Croatia and Spain, is in a rich vein of form.

Bellingham is pictured in a sharp suit and says he is inspired by iconic figures of yesteryear

The cover star feels a responsibility to be a gentleman and positive role model

Under Jose Mourinho's management at the Bernabeu this season, he's scored four goals and provided four assists already in LaLiga, with the Spanish giants three points behind Barcelona in the title race.

He's joined in the England squad by his younger brother, Jobe, and is flying high for the national side now his relationship with Tuchel is on an even keel.

Last Friday, the Three Lions manager said: 'It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course but we are in a good place.

'I love to be his coach. He's a top player, a very influential player and I think it goes both ways. If Jude was not feeling comfortable he would not perform on that level.

'In the moment you see he's happy to come into camp, he's happy with the role he has, he's fully invested and now to have the chance to have both of them is just the next step. I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach!'

On Jobe being called up from the Under-21s, he added: 'Yeah Jude and I have spoken about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream to play with Jobe for England.

'Jude was always saying: "Watch him, watch him he's good, he can make it". 'I would say: "Yeah we are watching him".

Bellingham poses in more casual attire, pairing a vintage Adidas sweater with pin stripe trousers

'I think he actually watched training very early in my reign. He came over and watched his brother train. We chatted and said it would be nice if one day he was with him.

'He was very kind and very polite and I'm glad to have him in camp. Everyone will compare them and he has to live with this.

'They look similar, even in their movements, but they are very different players. Jobe is more defensive. I think they are also different characters, at least that's what I heard.

'He couldn't stop smiling when I called to tell him the news. He has the same beautiful smile like Jude so it's nice to have him.'

#1362. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

Ryan Gravenberch is OFF 🟥 https://t.co/IVIHNzqw6k

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

They are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

But this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

Erling Haaland gives Manchester City the lead against Liverpool 🎯 https://t.co/cELo5y60Fk

In fact, Liverpool’s best performers were the young attackers Victor Muñoz and, making his first league start as a makeshift centre-forward, Lewis Koumas, who is just 21. Against that, City unleashed a battery of forward talent.

"Koumas & Munoz were better than the two £100million players!" Jamie Carragher is still disappointed with what he's seeing from Florian Wirtz in a Liverpool shirt 😬🔴 https://t.co/jJwOZbPJ4b

Was it an unfair advantage? It appears City have been thriving off that for some time and, while this team were not signed during the years the club have been found guilty of cheating, the argument is, of course, that they would not have joined without the sporting supremacy.

Certainly not Haaland, despite his avowed love for City. That cannot be doubted as his father, Alf-Inge, a former midfielder for the club, stood celebrating in the away end. The striker missed one chance when he should have scored, sent through on goal, shaking his head in disbelief at getting his angles wrong. It felt like a warning and that went unheeded as Doku, who had replaced one of their big summer signings in Iliman Ndiaye, cut in from the left with his shot deflecting into Haaland’s path. He made no mistake with a powerful, first-time finish.

Doku soon added a second, a sublime strike, as he dribbled goalwards, defenders backing off, and he arced a right-footed shot high beyond Alisson Becker’s grasp.

There were delighted chants of “olé” from the City supporters and that arrogance was rewarded by a strutting, emphatic third goal. It was finished by the mercurial Rayan Cherki after he was sent clear by a backheel from Josko Gvardiol, another substitute.

A moment of individual brilliance from Rayan Cherki to put the game beyond all doubt 🤯 https://t.co/wvmTMZcGhW

It captured City’s swagger, their sense of responding to what they regard as an injustice – that they maintain will be overturned on appeal – the sense they are going to continue to create an almighty headache for the Premier League. In a sea of uncertainty as to what will now happen, that is something we can be sure of.

“Cheats,” loudly boomed around Anfield from the home fans before the PA played Fleetwood Mac’s Tell Me Lies at the final whistle, as the players walked off. Those signs of defiance were not matched on the pitch. Although it may be a song City will get used to hearing for the rest of this extraordinary, unprecedented campaign.

Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

“You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”

Kerkez fires in a cross and there’s a miscommunication between Guehi and Donnarumma, with the centre-back slicing a clearance instead of allowing the goalkeeper to gather the delivery. Barcola can’t capitalise on the loose ball and City get away with one there.

There is a lot of noise but nothing has happened to light a fire and the onus has got to be on Liverpool’s players to step this up considerably. City motor forward on the counter through Cherki, whose delightful touch takes him away from Mac Allister. From inside his own half, the Frenchman dribbles to the edge of Liverpool’s penalty area. He attempts to play a one-two with Fernandez, but the pass is cut out by Jacquet.

Manchester City have not got going, as of yet. The defiant message from the club is they would not let the verdict affect them. They have defended well enough but have barely strung a passing sequence together against a Liverpool side who appear be playing off pure emotion.

Gravenberch is bossing this game in midfield. Another powerful run from deep results in a delightful nutmeg on Fernandez, who slips over. Liverpool’s energy has been really impressive. City need to ride out this early storm.

All fairly difficult to stomach, the Manchester City fans’ performance at kick-off. Inflatable bananas to signify nostalgia for the late 1980s, when these were all the rage after the club’s relegation to Division Two? The City of Sheikh Mansour are about as far removed from the era of Jimmy Frizzell as is possible to imagine, with their colossal wealth enabling cheating on an unprecedented scale. And as for the Poznan during You’ll Never Walk Alone? When Liam Gallagher asks Oasis fans to perform this backwards dance during next year’s tour, I suspect there will not be quite the same take-up.

There’s an early flashpoint as Koumas puts Guehi under serious pressure, causing the defender to fall to the ground and grab the ball with his hands. It’s not a foul and Liverpool are given a free kick. The hosts want Guehi booked and Araujo sprints over to the referee waving an imaginary yellow card, but gets one himself.

Amid all the build-up and backstory to this extraordinary fixture it is remarkable that 21-year-old Lewis Koumas is making his first Premier League start as Liverpool’s makeshift centre-forward. And he has started well.

A spell of Man City possession has slightly quelled the atmosphere. On paper, you would have to say the away side’s starting 11 is superior to Liverpool’s.

Liverpool make a fast start as Gravenberch effortlessly turns Fernandez and Munoz darts inside of O’Reilly. The winger’s shot is smothered by Guehi, but the early signs are encouraging for the hosts.

City get us under way at Anfield. This is one we’ve quite literally all been waiting for.

A roaring rendition of YNWA is bellowed by Anfield, which is in full voice. City players huddle together and go over to clap their fans in a show of solidarity.

In the corner of the stadium, where the Sir Kenny Dalglish Stand meets The Kop, there is a white banner with black paint proclaiming: “A generation of supporters cheated” - none of this is bothering the Manchester City fans, who are going back a generation and have a raft of inflatable bananas. (It was a craze in the 1980s, for you younger readers). Anyway, let’s get on with the game and what an opportunity this is for young Lewis Koumas, who has produced the individual performance of the season so far for Liverpool against Tottenham in the Carabao Cup. He needs to be a scampering, scurrying menace once again.

The Kop has now started a chant of “you cheating b-------” you know what you are. Doubt it will be the last time we hear that this afternoon. They are now singing “going down, going down, going down”.

No chance of hearing the names of the Manchester City players as the team is read out by the PA announcer. He is drowned out by the boos, jeers and whistles from the Liverpool fans. The atmosphere is certainly starting to build.

A re-imagining of Oasis’ Wonderwall at the front of the Kop. “And after all,” the banner reads, “you really robbed us all.”

Andoni Iraola told Sky Sports: “He came back from the international break with an overload. He felt a tight hamstring.

“He tried somehow pushing through training, but he was not feeling 100 per cent.

With just over 15 minutes until kick-off, here’s a recap of the two sides.

Liverpool: Alisson, Araujo, Jacquet, van Dijk, Kerkez, Gravenberch, Mac Allister, Barcola, Wirtz, Munoz, Koumas.

When asked if the mindset and mood are right for him to do his job, the City boss replied: “Yes. Absolutely. Yes.

“The mood is good, the mindset is good. Now it’s time to start the game - finally!

“It [togetherness] is very important; the mix between the players and the fans, everyone.

“We are away in a complicated environment, a complicated stadium, but we are going to do our best to try to win the game.”

The Manchester City players are out for their warm-up and, dare it be said, they were greeted with apathy by the Liverpool fans. Not even the murmur of a boo when Erling Haaland and Co emerged. It surely will be very different when kick off comes.

The current City players found themselves in a peculiar situation as none of this is their fault, but they’ll be the ones who receive the brunt of abuse from rival fans as the public-facing figures of the club. They’ll need to be braced for a hostile reception at every away ground in England.

However, you can expect Anfield to turn up the heat to one of the highest levels, given how alleged City’s actions have impacted Liverpool’s trophy haul.

Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool finished second in the 2018-19 season, accumulating a staggering 98 points, while winning 30 matches and losing just once. City incredibly pipped them to the Premier League trophy by one point. A strikingly similar scenario occurred in the 2021-22 campaign, with Liverpool placing as runners-up with 92 points. You guessed it, City had 93.

What’s done is done, and ultimately we are entering a territory of ifs, buts and maybes. However, if City’s appeal against the charges is unsuccessful and the guilty verdict is upheld, then Liverpool would have unfairly missed out on historic success and lifelong memories.

News breaks that City had been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules.

Telegraph Sport understands that Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal and Tottenham Hotspur were contacted in advance of the email to the other 15 clubs.

In a letter to fans, a defiant Khaldoon Al Mubarak, City’s chairman, expresses complete confidence that his club would be vindicated.

“There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club,” he writes. “We will not give them that opportunity.”

With the football world still making sense of the news, Tony Pulis admits to feeling “cheated”. His Stoke City side were defeated by Manchester City in the 2011 FA Cup final, during the 2009-23 period.

Hull City owner Acun Ilicali then likens City’s transgressions to “doping” before Mauricio Pochettino, whose Spurs side were often in the hunt with City for major trophies during his time as manager, says that football has “lived through a period of deception”.

The Premier League reveals that City’s owners inflated “sham” sponsorship deals by £830.69m between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

It also discloses that image rights had been inflated and key witnesses had lied.

Ferran Soriano, chief executive of City Football Group, appears helpless when questioned about the verdict’s findings at the European Football Clubs’ general assembly in Copenhagen by Sky News.

An unblinking Soriano then features in a video statement published by City in which he claimed their guilty verdict was based on “a single false accusation”.

With City on the ropes, Pep Guardiola releases a statement in support of his former club, assuring supporters that “we will get through this together”.

The Prime Minister says that he would be “really concerned” to lose City’s owners, but after significant backlash, No 10 moves to clarify his reaction saying that “if wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences”.

It later amends the statement to “wherever wrongdoing is established”.

The UAE then warns Andy Burnham that it will pull billions of pounds of investment out of the UK in retaliation for the guilty verdict against City.

City argue that their sponsorship deals were part-funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club’s owners, in their appeal, which claims bank statements and witness accounts provide “irrefutable evidence” to support their case.
